'''betear''' (bē-tēr′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''tear''<sup>2</sup>.] To wet with tears. ''Sir P. Sidney.''

'''beteche†''', ''v. t.'' Same as ''beteach.''

'''beteem<sup>1</sup>†''' (bē-tēm′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''teem''<sup>1</sup>.] To bring forth; produce; shed.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Lys.'' Why is your cheek so pale?
How chance the roses there do fade so fast?
''Her.'' Belike for want of rain; which I could well
''Beteem'' them from the tempest of mine eyes.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., i. 1.}}}}

'''beteem<sup>2</sup>†''' (bē-tēm′), ''v. t.'' [Appar. < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''teem''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' To allow; permit; suffer.
{{smaller block|<poem>So loving to my mother,
That he might not ''beteem'' the winds of heaven
Visit her face too roughly. ''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 2.</poem>}}
'''2.''' To vouchsafe; accord; give.
{{smaller block|“So would I,” said the Enchanter, “glad and faine ''Beteeme'' to you this sword.” ''Spenser'', F. Q., II. viii. 19.}}
{{smaller block|Although hee could have well ''beteem’d'' to have thankt him of the ease hee profer’d, yet loving his owne handiworke, modestly refus’d him.
{{right|''Milton'', Def. of Humb. Remonst.}}}}

''betel, bethel, betelhe'', formerly also ''betle, vitele'', < Malayalam ''vettila'' = Tamil ''vettilei'' (cerebral ''t''), betel; cf. Hind. ''bīrā'' or ''bīrī'',

< Skt. ''vitika'' (cerebral ''t''), betel.] '''1.''' A species of pepper, ''Piper betle'', a creeping or climbing plant, a native of the East Indies, natural order ''Piperaceæ.'' {{smaller|The leaves are used as a wrapper for the little pellets of areca-nut and lime which are extensively chewed in the East. The pellet is hot and acrid, but has aromatic and astringent properties. It tinges the saliva red and blackens the teeth. Also called ''betel-pepper.''}} '''2.''' A piece of betel-nut.

'''betel-box''' (bē′tl-boks), ''n.'' A box for carrying pellets prepared of betel-leaves, lime, and areca-nuts. Such boxes are commonly made of silver filigree.

[[FIGURE]]
{{c|{{smaller|Areca-palm (''Areca Catechu''), with its fruit, the Betel-nut.}}}}

'''betel-nut''' (bē′tl-nut), ''n.'' [< ''betel'' + ''nut.''] The nut of the areca-palm, ''Areca Catechu'', of the East Indies, highly esteemed among the Asiatics as a masticatory. See ''areca-nut.''

'''betel-pepper''' (bē′tl-pep″ėr), ''n.'' Same as ''betel'', 1.

'''beth†''', ''v. i. impv.'' [ME., < AS. ''beóth'', 2d pers. pl. of ''beón'', be: see ''be.''] Be ye. ''Chaucer.''

'''bethankit''' (bē-thang′kit), ''n.'' [Sc., humorously adapted from the formula ''God be thankit'', where ''thankit'' = E. ''thanked'', pp.] Grace after meat. ''Burns.''
readings.c1s3:
¶
'''bethel''' (beth′el), ''n.'' [Heb. ''bēth-ēl'', house of God, < ''bēth'', house, + ''ēl'', God; hence ''Bethel'' (''Beth-el''), name of a place: see ''Elohim''.] '''1.''' A hallowed spot.—'''2.''' A name sometimes applied to a place of worship in England, especially to a dissenting chapel.—'''3.''' A church or chapel for seamen, whether located on shore or, as is often the case, afloat in a harbor.

'''Bethell process.''' See ''process''.

'''bethink''' (bẹ̄-thingk′), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''bethought'', ppr. ''bethinking''. [< ME. ''bethenken'', ''bithinken'', commonly ''bethenchen'', < AS. ''bethencan'', ''bithencan'' (= D. ''bedenken'' = OHG. ''bidenchan'', MHG. G. ''bedenken'' = Sw. ''betänka'' = Dan. ''betænke''), consider, think about, < ''be-'' + ''thencan'', think: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''think''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To think; imagine.
{{smaller block|He spak more harm than herte may ''bethinke''.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Wife of Bath’s Tale, l. 772.}}}}
'''2†.''' To think about; reflect upon; consider.
{{smaller block|<poem>With patience calm the storm,
While we ''bethink'' a means to break it off.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., iii. 3.}}}}
'''3.''' Reflexively: (''a'') To call to mind; take into consideration; remind one’s self: with ''of'' (formerly also ''on'' or ''upon'') before the name of the object of thought.
{{smaller block|''Bethink yourselves'' beforehand what mercies you want.
{{right|''Bp. Beveridge'', Sermons, II. cxlv.}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>Who healed again the smitten ear,
And sheathed his follower’s sword.</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', The Exiles.}}}}
(''b'') To reflect; deliberate; commune with one’s self.
{{smaller block|Rip ''bethought himself'' a moment and inquired.
{{right|''Irving'', Sketch-Book, p. 60.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To deliberate; consider.
{{smaller block|''Bethink'' ere thou dismiss us. ''Byron'', Manfred, i. 1.}}

'''Bethlehem''' (beth′lẹ̄-ẹm), ''n.'' See ''bedlam.''

'''Bethlehemite''' (beth′lẹ̄-ẹm-īt), ''n.'' [< ''Bethlehem'' + ''-ite''<sup>1</sup>. See ''bedlam.''] '''1.''' An inhabitant of Bethlehem of Judea (2 Sam. xxi. 19).—'''2.''' An inmate of Bethlehem hospital or other lunatic asylum; a bedlamite. See ''bedlam'' and ''bedlamite.''—'''3.''' ''Eccles.'': (''a'') One of an order of monks introduced into England in the year 1257, who were habited like the Dominicans, except that they wore a star with five rays, in memory of the comet or star which appeared over Bethlehem at the birth of Christ. (''b'') One of an order founded in the seventeenth century for the service of the hospitals in Spanish America.

'''Bethlemite†''' (beth′lẹm-īt), ''n.'' Same as ''Bethlehemite.''

'''bethought''' (bẹ̄-thôt′). Preterit and past participle of ''bethink.''

'''bethrall''' (bẹ̄-thrâl′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''thrall.''] To enslave; reduce to bondage; bring into subjection.
{{smaller block|She it is that did my Lord ''bethrall.''
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. viii. 28.}}}}

'''bethroot''' (beth′röt), ''n.'' Same as ''birthroot.''

''Eccles.'': (''a'') One of an order of monks introduced into England in the year 1257, who were habited like the Dominicans, except that they wore a star with five rays, in memory of the comet or star which appeared over Bethlehem at the birth of Christ. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. viii. 28.}}}}

'''bethroot''' (beth′röt), ''n.'' Same as ''birthroot.''

'''bethule''' (beth′ūl), ''n.''   [< ''Bethylus.'']   A bird of the genus ''Bethylus'' (Cuvier), or ''Cissopis'' (Vieillot).

'''bethump''' (bẹ̄-thump′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''thump.'']   To beat soundly.
{{smaller block|<poem>I was never so ''bethump’d'' with words
Since I first call’d my brother’s father dad.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, ii. 2.}}}}

'''bethwack''' (bē-thwak′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''thwack.'']   To thrash soundly.

'''Bethylus''' (beth′i-lus), ''n.''   [NL.]   '''1.''' A genus of pupivorous hymenopterous insects, of the family ''Proctotrypidæ'', having an elongated and somewhat triangular prothorax, a flattened head, and 13-jointed antennæ.—'''2.''' In ''ornith.'', a genus of South American tanagroid ''Passeres'', based on the ''Lanius leverianus'' of Shaw, supposed to be a shrike. {{smaller|Antedated by ''Cissopis'' of Vieillot, 1816, based upon the same bird, and also in entomology. Also spelled ''Bethyllus.'' [Not in use.]}}

'''betide''' (bẹ̄-tīd′), ''v.''   [< ME. ''bitiden'', < ''bi-'', ''be-'', + ''tiden'', happen: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''tide'', ''v.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To happen; befall; come to.
{{smaller block|What will ''betide'' the few? {{right|''Milton'', P. L., xii. 480.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>“Ill luck ''betide'' them all”—he cried.</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', The Exiles.}}}}
'''2.''' To betoken; signify. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>How could I but muse
At what such a dream should ''betide''?</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', The Morning Dream.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To come to pass; happen.—'''To betide on†''', {{smaller|to become of.}}
{{smaller block|If he were dead, what would ''betide on'' me?
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., i. 3.}}}}

'''betide†''' (bẹ̄-tīd′), ''n.''   [< ''betide, v.'']   Hap; fortune. —{{smaller|'''Bad betide†''', ill hap; misfortune: a forced use.}}
{{smaller block|My wretched heart wounded with ''bad betide.''
{{right|''Greene'', Francesco’s Sonnet.}}}}

'''betight†''' (bẹ̄-tīt′). An erroneously formed past participle of ''betide:'' one of Spenser’s forced forms.
{{smaller block|<poem>Why wayle we then? why weary we the Gods with playnts,
As if some evill were to her ''betight?''</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Shep. Cal., November.}}}}

'''betime†''' (bẹ̄-tīm′), ''adv.'', orig. ''prep. phr.''   [< ME. ''betyme, bitime'', prop. separate, ''bi time'', by time.]   Older form of ''betimes.''
{{smaller block|<poem>Loke thou go to bede ''by tyme.''</poem>
{{right|''How the Goode Wyfe Taught hyr Doughter'', l. 165.}}}}
{{smaller block|All in the morning ''betime.'' ''Shak.'', Hamlet, iv. 5 (song).

I went one day myself ''betime'' in the morning to a great man’s house to speak with him.
{{right|''Latimer'', Serm. bef. Edw. VI., 1550.}}}}

'''betimes''' (bẹ̄-tīmz′), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''betymes, bitymes'', < ''betime'' + adv. gen. suffix ''-s.'']   '''1.''' Seasonably; in good season or time; before it is too late; early.
{{smaller block|Not to be a-bed after midnight is to be up ''betimes.''
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., ii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>To measure life learn thou ''betimes.''</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Sonnets, xvi.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Partake we their blithe cheer
Who gathered in ''betimes'' the unshorn flock
To wash the fleece. ''Wordsworth'', River Duddon, xxiii.</poem>}}
{{smaller block|we set out ''betimes'' this morning for Olevano.
{{right|''Lowell'', Fireside Travels, p. 240.}}}}

'''2.''' Soon; in a short time.
{{smaller block|He tires ''betimes'', that spurs too fast betimes.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., ii. 1.}}}}
'''3.''' Occasionally; at times. [Scotch.] ='''Syn.''' {{smaller|''Early, Soon, Betimes.'' See ''early''.}}

'''betine†''', ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''tine'' for ''tind'', kindle.]   To set fire to.

'''betit†''', ''v.'' Obsolete shortened form of ''betideth''.   ''Chaucer.''

'''betitle''' (bẹ̄-tī′tl), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''title''.]   To give a title or titles to; entitle: as, a ''betitled'' man; a “picture . . . ''betitled'', Glorious Revolution,” ''Carlyle'', Misc., III. 82.

'''betle''', ''n.'' See ''betel''.

'''betoil†''' (bē-toil′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''toil''<sup>1</sup>.]   To worry with toil.

'''betok†'''. Middle English preterit of ''betake''<sup>2</sup>.

'''betoken''' (bẹ̄-tō′kn), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''betokenen'', ''bitocnen'', < AS. *''betācnian'' (not found; equiv. to ''getācnian'', with diff. prefix; cf. ''believe'') (= OFries. ''bitekna'' = D. ''beteekenen'' = LG. ''beteiken'' = OHG. ''bizeichanōn'', G. ''bezeichnen'' = Sw. ''beteckna'' = Dan. ''betegne''), < ''be-'' + ''tācn'', ''tācen'', token: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''token''.]   '''1†.''' To signify; mean; denote in words.—'''2.''' To be a token of; be a visible sign of; give promise of.
{{smaller block|A dewy cloud, and in the cloud a bow, . . .
''Betokening'' peace from God. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., xi. 867.}}}}

'''3.''' To foreshow by signs; be or furnish a premonition of; indicate the probability of: as, this fact ''betokens'' a good result.
{{smaller block|The morning ''betokened'' foul weather.
{{right|''Bancroft'', Hist. Const., II. 261.}}}}
'''4.''' To give evidence of; show.
{{smaller block|<poem>This doth ''betoken''
The corse they follow did with desperate hand
Fordo its own life. {{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, v. 1.}}</poem>}}
='''Syn.''' {{smaller|To signify; presage, portend, augur, bode.}}

'''beton''' (bet′on; F. pron. bā-tôṅ′), ''n.''   [< F. ''béton'', < OF. ''betun'', rubble, of disputed origin, but prob. < Pr. ''beton'' = Sp. ''betun'', < L. ''bitumen'', bitumen: see ''bitumen''. Some compare F. ''beton'', beestings, curded milk, < OF. ''beter'', coagulate.]   A mixture of lime, sand, and gravel, forming a kind of concrete. {{smaller|It is much used as a hydraulic cement in submarine works, and whole buildings have been constructed of it.}}

'''betongue''' (bẹ̄-tung′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''tongue''.]   To scold; attack with the tongue; rail at.
{{smaller block|How Ben Jonson and Shakspere ''betongued'' each other.
{{right|''North British Rev.''}}}}

'''betonica''' (be-ton′i-kä), ''n.'' Same as ''betony''.

'''betony''' (bet′ọ-ni), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''betonie'', ''bettony'', etc., < ME. ''betony'', ''betany'', earlier ''betone'', ''betan'' (cf. ML. ''betonia''), < OF. ''beteine'', F. ''bétoine'' = Pr. Sp. Pg. It. ''betonica'' = G. ''betonie'' = AS. ''betonica'', < L. ''betonica'', a corrupt form of ''vettonica'', so named, according to Pliny, from the ''Vettones'', otherwise ''Vectones'', a people of Lusitania in the Spanish peninsula.]   The popular name of ''Stachys Betonica'' or ''Betonica officinalis'', a European labiate plant, growing in woods. {{smaller|It is sometimes used to dye wool, producing a dark-yellow color. It is usually distinguished from ''water-betony'' (an aquatic plant, ''Scrophularia aquatica'') as ''wood-betony'', which name is also given in the United States to ''Pedicularis Canadensis'', and sometimes to ''Lycopus Virginicus''. The ''Veronica serpyllifolia'' is called ''Paul’s betony'', because described as a betony by an old herbalist, Paulus Ægineta.}}
